lead: A virtual object is stored in two parts. Geometry records the shape: where the surface sits in space. Appearance records how that surface looks: its colour, shine and pattern. The headset draws nothing until both parts exist. A helmet with the right shape but no material looks like grey plastic; a rich material on the wrong shape still looks wrong. Modelling is the step that writes both parts into the scene file, before transforms, physics or rendering touch the object. The rendering pipeline reads this data later.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, components of a VR system, and comfort with 3D coordinates (x, y, z), plus the idea of a scene file from model management.

sections.h3: Shape stored as a polygon mesh

blocks.text: Shape is stored as a polygon mesh. A mesh has three records. A vertex is a point in space, written as three numbers (x, y, z) in metres. An edge joins two vertices. A face is a closed loop of edges that encloses a flat area. Graphics hardware draws triangles, so faces are triangles or are split into triangles.

A triangle stores three vertex indices. Two triangles that share a corner store that corner once in the vertex array. Both triangles refer to it from the index array. This is an indexed mesh. A grid of 100 × 100 quads has 10,201 shared vertices and 20,000 triangles.
A normal is a unit vector at right angles to a surface. It tells the shader which way the surface faces. The face normal comes from the cross product of two triangle edges.
n = (v<sub>1</sub> − v<sub>0</sub>) × (v<sub>2</sub> − v<sub>0</sub>), then n̂ = n ÷ |n|
blocks.where: v<sub>0</sub>, v<sub>1</sub>, v<sub>2</sub> are the corner positions in metres; × is the cross product; |n| is the length of n; n̂ is the unit face normal.

blocks.text: Tessellation splits a coarse polygon into smaller triangles. It rounds a curved silhouette and adds detail near the camera. Steps to build a mesh: (1) list the vertices, (2) list triangles as index triples, (3) compute face and vertex normals, (4) tessellate where smoothness is needed.

sections.h3: Curves, surfaces, implicit shapes, voxels and points

blocks.text: Not every shape is a triangle mesh. A parametric curve is a point that moves with one number t. A Bézier curve is P(t) = Σ Bi(t) Pi for t in [0, 1]. Pi are control points in metres; Bi(t) are blending functions. The curve is smooth and stays inside the convex hull of its control points. A designer places a few control points to get a car body line.
A parametric surface uses two numbers (u, v). It maps a flat square of parameters into 3D. This is how a helmet shell or a chair seat is modelled before it is tessellated into triangles.

An implicit surface is written as f(x, y, z) = 0. A sphere of radius r centred at the origin is x² + y² + z² − r² = 0. The sign of f tells inside from outside in one test. Metaballs and smooth blends between shapes use this form.

A voxel is a small cube in a regular 3D grid. Each voxel stores whether it is filled, or a density value. Medical scans arrive this way. Point clouds are unordered lists of 3D points from a depth camera or laser scanner. They have no faces and no normals, so a meshing step is needed before ordinary rendering.

Appearance is stored as material values plus texture data. A material describes how the surface responds to light. Diffuse colour is the base colour seen under broad light. It is stored as three floats, one each for red, green and blue, usually from 0 to 1. Specular level sets the strength of the bright highlight. Roughness sets how spread out that highlight is: a low value gives a sharp dot, a high value gives a broad sheen.

Texture is a 2D image laid over the surface. UV mapping gives every vertex a pair (u, v). Both numbers lie between 0 and 1, whatever the image size in pixels. The rasteriser interpolates u and v across each triangle and reads the image at that point. Vertices store the coordinates, never the whole image.

A shader is a small program that combines these inputs with the lights. A vertex shader can pass normals and UVs forward; a fragment shader can look up the texture and compute the diffuse plus specular colour. Unit 5 covers writing shaders.

spec.aria: A square split by a diagonal into two triangles, its four corners labelled v0 to v3 with UV coordinates; beside it four boxes of 48, 32, 12 and 12 bytes summing to 104.

examples.question: A square wall is stored as two triangles sharing four vertices. Each vertex stores a position (3 floats) and a UV pair (2 floats); each float is 4 bytes. Each triangle stores three uint16 indices. The wall material stores diffuse colour as 3 floats. Find the total bytes.
steps: Number of vertices = 4; number of triangles = 2.
Position bytes = 4 vertices × 3 floats × 4 bytes = 48 B.
UV bytes = 4 vertices × 2 floats × 4 bytes = 32 B.
Index bytes = 2 triangles × 3 indices × 2 bytes = 12 B (uint16 is 2 bytes).
Diffuse colour bytes = 3 floats × 4 bytes = 12 B.

v = 4
pos = v * 3 * 4
uv = v * 2 * 4
idx = 2 * 3 * 2
col = 3 * 4
print(pos)
print(uv)
print(idx)
print(col)
print(pos + uv + idx + col)

traps: Counting one vertex per triangle: shared corners are stored once and reused through the index buffer.
Mixing float count with byte count: 3 floats is 12 bytes, not 3 bytes.
Storing a full texture image at every vertex: a vertex carries only its (u, v) coordinates.
Treating a normal as a position: a normal is a direction, not a point in metres.
Forgetting that a quad wall is two triangles when counting indices.

quiz.q: Name the three records of a polygon mesh.
quiz.a: Vertices (points), edges (pairs of vertices), faces (closed loops of edges).

quiz.q: What do u and v mean in UV mapping?
quiz.a: Coordinates in [0, 1] giving a position inside the texture image.

quiz.q: Why store vertices once and list triangles as indices?
quiz.a: Shared corners are reused, which saves memory; shared normals also stay consistent at a corner.

quiz.q: A cube has 8 vertices and 12 triangles. Each vertex has a position (3 floats) and a UV pair (2 floats); a float is 4 bytes. Each triangle has 3 uint16 indices. Find the total bytes.
An implicit sphere is x² + y² + z² − 0.25 = 0, in metres. Find its radius and decide whether the point (0.1, 0.1, 0.1) is inside.
Two wall models have identical vertex positions but one renders dull and flat. Name two appearance fields that could explain it.
quiz.a: Diffuse colour could be darker; specular level could be zero or roughness high; the texture could be missing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production pipelines use subdivision surfaces such as Catmull–Clark to turn a coarse cage into a smooth shape, and displacement maps to push real geometric detail into a surface at render time. Gaussian splatting and neural radiance fields store appearance as learned radiance rather than a mesh plus texture, and they are moving into real-time VR viewers. Search terms: glTF, Pixar OpenSubdiv, PBR metallic-roughness, NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting.
